1	# Blog voice
2	
3	How posts under `src/content/blog/` should read. Reference example: `shopifys-aquifer-in-the-open.mdx`.
4	
5	The target is the voice of Shopify's "Under the River" engineering post, written in first person. Confident, plain, technical without posturing. Sounds like an engineer explaining a real opinion to peers, not a marketing page and not an essay.
6	
7	## Do
8	
9	- **Open with an opinion, not a summary.** Take a position in the first two paragraphs. Disagree with something. If the post only restates a source, it has no reason to exist.
10	- **Short declarative sentences, varied with longer ones.** Let a fragment land for emphasis: "That is the easy version." "A product does."
11	- **Repeat the key noun** instead of reaching for synonyms. "The corpus", "the memory", "the session". Repetition builds the through-line.
12	- **Open each section with a constraint or fact, then pivot to the insight.**
13	- **First person.** "We made the same bet." "I wrote about that split in..." Own the claim.
14	- **Argue with specifics.** Name the table, the mechanism, the real difference. Vague beats nothing, specific beats vague.
15	- **Plain, slightly declarative headers.** Statements or mild antithesis: "The corpus is the asset. The conversation isn't." Not clever, not cute.
16	
17	## Don't
18	
19	- **No em dashes.** Hard rule for all landing copy. Use periods, commas, or parentheses. This also forces the staccato rhythm we want.
20	- **No three-beat marketing chants.** "Your agent. Your data. Your servers." is the single clearest AI tell. Kill it on sight.
21	- **No rhetorical questions** as a transition ("So why store the noise?").
22	- **No stacked tricolons** or relentless "not X, but Y" balance in every paragraph. One antithesis per stretch, not five.
23	- **No clever-for-clever's-sake** word pairs ("noise vs signal", "same goal, different cut", "strictly harder"). They read as filler.
24	- **No hedging AI filler:** "it's worth noting", "on one hand / on the other", "in today's world".
25	- **Don't paraphrase the source** section by section. Engage two or three points with depth instead of touring all of them.
26	
27	## Shape
28	
29	- Comparison or opinion posts: roughly 600 to 700 words.
30	- 3 to 5 sentences per paragraph, rarely longer.
31	- Quote a source verbatim when it sharpens the point, but keep quotes short.
32	
33	## The test
34	
35	Read it out loud. If a line sounds like a slide deck or a press release, rewrite it. If it sounds like you talking, keep it.

2	title: "Shopify's Aquifer, in the Open"
3	description: "Shopify treats an agent's corpus as the compounding asset. Lobu keeps the signal—not the chat—and makes that architecture work across companies."
4	date: 2026-05-29
5	author: Burak Emre Kabakcı
6	authorUrl: https://x.com/bu7emba
7	tags: [architecture, agents, memory]
8	cover: /design/tabfig-memory.webp
9	draft: false
10	---
11	
12	Shopify published [Under the River](https://shopify.engineering/under-the-river), the writeup of the substrate they built so agents could become real participants in how they ship code. Read past the Slack bot and there's a bet. They state it plainly: "the corpus is the compounding asset; the privacy of an agent thread is a disadvantage."
13	
14	We made the same bet. An agent that only helps the person at the keyboard is autocomplete. An agent that learns from everyone is infrastructure. The disagreement is narrow, and it is about what you write down.
15	
16	## The corpus is the asset. The conversation isn't.
17	
18	River is public by default. The threads pile up in Slack, stay searchable, and the patterns get fed back into River's skills later. The corpus is the chat. The signal gets pulled out after the fact.
19	
20	We don't keep the chat. We keep what the chat was about. Every interaction becomes an event in an append-only log: structured, embedded, searchable. Extraction happens once, at write time, instead of every time you read. The conversation is scaffolding. The event is the thing that lasts.
21	
22	This is the warehouse, not the notebook. I wrote about that split in [Filesystem vs Database for Agent Memory](/blog/filesystem-vs-database-agent-memory/). The filesystem is where the agent thinks. The memory layer is where the company remembers.
23	
24	Shopify are halfway here. River writes its own sessions to a `river_sessions` table. We have a table too. The difference is that ours is not a log bolted onto one agent. In Lobu the events log is the platform. Every agent reads it and writes it. They share one memory. A new agent inherits the whole history instead of starting on an empty table.
25	
26	## One memory. Everyone.
27	
28	This is what turns a fast assistant into a useful one. You ask, and it already knows. The colleague who hit the same wall last week. The decision made in another channel. The customer a sales thread mentioned. One agent, one company memory, and it gets denser every day the company shows up.
29	
30	## One company is the easy version
31	
32	Under the River never says the word "organization." It doesn't have to. Everything lives inside Shopify. One company, one corpus, shared by default.
33	
34	That is the easy version. The hard one is many companies at once. The memory stays separate per org. The credentials per tenant. All on the same machines, and no org's agent ever touches another's data. That is the real work, and it is what Lobu is built around. Each org gets its own memory that compounds, on shared infrastructure, walled off from the rest. A single company never has to solve this. A product does.
35	
36	## Keep the agent away from the secrets
37	
38	Their first lesson is to keep the harness out of the sandbox. The agent loop should not live where the code runs, so a bad turn has a small blast radius. We agree, and we draw a second line. The worker never holds a real secret. A proxy sits in front of it and swaps placeholder tokens for the real ones only as a request leaves the box. The agent uses credentials it never sees and can never leak.
39	
40	## The difference
41	
42	River runs inside Shopify and that is where it stays. Lobu is the version you run yourself. Same memory, same agent everyone talks to, except the database stays under your control and model traffic follows the providers you configure. The only thing we really had to add is the part where it holds up for many companies on one install, not one company that owns the whole place.
43	
44	Start with the [docs](/getting-started/), or read how the [memory layer](/getting-started/memory/) works.
45

1	---
2	title: "The Context Layer Is an Event Store"
3	description: "Tasman says no product can build your context layer because the content doesn't exist. Half right. The governed why is a versioned, access-controlled event store that mirrors the warehouse instead of replacing it — and I built the Kelder scenario to find where that holds and where it doesn't."
4	date: 2026-07-12
5	author: Burak Emre Kabakcı
6	authorUrl: https://x.com/bu7emba
7	tags: [architecture, agents, memory, analytics]
8	draft: false
9	---
10	
11	Tasman Analytics published [How to build a context layer](https://www.tasman.ai/news/how-to-build-a-context-layer), the best writeup yet of a failure everyone running data agents has seen. The semantic layer is the governed what. Nobody wrote down the governed why. So the agent computes churn correctly, sees a spike in March, and invents an explanation, because the billing migration that wrote 1,900 fake cancellations was never stored anywhere a machine can read.
12	
13	The numbers behind this are brutal. Anthropic found the same model went from at most 21% correct to over 95% on their internal analytics once it had the right skills around it: procedural routing, reference files, a governed data foundation. Then accuracy fell back toward 65% within a month as the underlying models drifted and nobody kept the skill docs current. In that system the limiting variable was the context, not the model.
14	
15	Tasman's conclusion is that no product can solve this, because the content does not exist yet. It lives in analysts' heads and scrolled Slack threads. I agree that it is a workflow problem. I think the governed *why* wants one substrate, not four.
16	
17	## The governed why wants one substrate
18	
19	Their design spreads the why across four homes: column caveats in dbt YAML, a business_events table in the warehouse, decision records as markdown in git, and verified queries pinned in the semantic layer. Four systems, four maintenance rituals, glued together by three MCP servers and the model's context window.
20	
21	I don't think all four collapse into one product, and I want to be honest about which parts don't. A dbt caveat belongs next to the model so the code and the caveat change in the same commit. A verified query belongs where routing uses it. Those have a source of truth and it isn't Lobu. But they can be *mirrored* into one queryable place through connectors, the way you'd sync any source, so an agent reads one store instead of stitching three MCP servers together at answer time. Mirroring is not the same as owning. The authoritative copy stays where the authoring workflow lives.
22	
23	What genuinely does want to live in one store is the part nobody owns today: the dated business events, the definition changelog, and the decisions. We took Tasman's fictional company, Kelder Coffee, and built that overlay on Lobu without changing a line of Lobu. A `business-event` entity type holds the migration, the definition change, the courier strike, each with affected metrics and a link to the incident. The changelog is not a table anyone maintains. Events in Lobu are append-only and versioned by supersession, so saving churn v2 with a pointer to v1 *is* the changelog. Query the current definition or the full history, same store.
24	
25	The live series is never materialized. A read-only connector runs the churn rollup live against the customer's own Postgres, and a sandboxed script joins that series with the business events and the definition versions in plain JavaScript. The context doesn't just annotate the numbers, it *drives the query*. March reads raw 550, and the billing-migration event carries a structured adjustment, so the script subtracts the ~500 artifact rows and reports 50 — the real cancellations that month still stand, the month isn't thrown away. The churn definition's v2 (a dunning-grace exclusion) is a `WHERE` fragment the script applies per month, so a month after the v2 boundary is counted at 38 where v1 would have said 50 — same warehouse, different number, because the definition changed the query and not just the label. Every deviation cites its source. No model in the loop.
26	
27	That is a deterministic composition, and it proves seeded context can be composed into a sourced answer. It does not yet prove an agent *retrieves* the right context and writes the right query on its own — the repo ships that eval, WITH-context versus baseline, and it passes as a deterministic proxy; the live-agent run just needs a model key wired in. I'm calling that out rather than dressing the proxy up as the real thing.
28	
29	The trust loop is a pinned verified query: store the approved answer, re-run the SQL later, diff the rows. When the warehouse moves under a definition, the rows change and the diff fires before someone repeats a stale number in a board deck. It is a result-drift canary, not a measure of whether an agent stayed accurate. Those are different failures and the honest version says so.
30	
31	The runnable example is in the repo (link goes live when the PRs below land).
32	
33	## Capture is an ingestion problem, not a documentation problem
34	
35	"The content does not exist yet" is the strongest line in their piece, and their fix is PR templates and incident runbooks. Asking humans to write documentation is how we got here.
36	
37	The why gets spoken exactly once, in a Slack thread, at the moment the CFO agrees to exclude returns from revenue. Lobu's watchers already sit in those threads. Capturing that sentence as a decision event, typed, dated, linked back to the thread, is ingestion. The human approves it instead of authoring it. That is the difference between a context layer that fills up and a wiki that rots.
38	
39	## Context has to be pushed, not searched
40	
41	An agent that doesn't know March is poisoned has no reason to search for "is March poisoned." The jump from 21 to 95 comes from context sitting in the prompt before the first query gets written, not from a retrieval the agent thinks to run.
42	
43	This one we had to fix in our own house. Entity-type and field descriptions were stored in Lobu and never rendered into the instructions agents receive, so we render them now, and we added a `guidance` event kind: org-level context that admins author and every agent sees on every request. The data model is just an event, which is the nice part, editing guidance means superseding it and the history of your own operating instructions is more memory. But storing it is the easy half. Rendering it, gating who can author it, capping how much lands in the prompt, and injecting it safely is the actual work, and that was a real branch, not a config flag. A prompt budget also means this can't hold arbitrary org context, so selective retrieval doesn't go away, it sits underneath.
44	
45	One more thing nobody in this conversation mentions: access control. The moment real decisions go into a shared layer, "who may see this why" is the first question an enterprise asks. Lobu compiles per-connection and per-resource visibility straight into the query SQL, so a private connection's data or a repo you're not a member of never surfaces in a coworker's answer. Arbitrary per-decision authorization is further out, but having the fence compiled into the read path rather than bolted on afterward is the part that's genuinely hard to retrofit.
46	
47	What's honestly still missing is more than plumbing. Warehouse connectors in cloud needed real egress hardening before we could open them, and that landed. Lineage from a dbt manifest needs an SPI addition. Federated metric definitions from Cube or Snowflake are designed and not wired, and reflecting them means the metric compiler can't assume Postgres dialect. Beyond our own code: the Slack-to-decision capture I described is the design, not a shipped demo, and the harder-than-storage question of whether a captured sentence is actually an authoritative, correctly-scoped decision is editorial judgment a human still makes. And the agent eval passes as a deterministic proxy today; the live-agent version, an actual model answering the March question with the context pushed versus without, needs a provider key wired in and is the honest remaining gap. So the honest claim is narrow: the governed why is a small, versioned, access-controlled event store, and it mirrors the semantic layer and the warehouse rather than replacing them. That is a component, not a fifth product you buy, and you can run it today.
48	
49	*Also worth reading: Tasman's [semantic vs. context essay](https://www.tasman.ai/news/we-are-still-confusing-the-semantic-layer-for-context-its-not), Yali Sassoon on [why a semantic layer is not a context layer](https://datacreation.substack.com/p/a-semantic-layer-is-not-a-context), and Snowflake's [agent context layer](https://www.snowflake.com/en/blog/agent-context-layer-trustworthy-data-agents/).*

People often ask the wrong question:

**Should agent memory live in the filesystem or in a database?**

My background is in data systems, so I think about this the same way I think about analytics infrastructure.

A company does not run on analysts' notebooks alone, and it does not ask analysts to do all of their work directly in warehouse tables. It needs both:

- operational systems to run the business
- a central warehouse to accumulate durable facts
- analysts using SQL and Python to make sense of raw data
- curated tables that business users can consume in BI tools

- the **filesystem** is where the agent does temporary work

Here is how to build and own one with Lobu." date: 2026-06-21 author: Burak Emre Kabakcı authorUrl: https://x.com/bu7emba tags: [agents, architecture, loops, saas] cover: /design/auto-radar.webp draft: false --- import { EventLoopAnimation } from "../../components/blog/EventLoopAnimation"; import { Tweet } from "../../components/blog/Tweet";

TL;DR: The workflow layer above your systems of record, the part you used to buy a tool for, is becoming agent loops you build. A loop that watches your data and acts is that business logic, built once on one backend with shared memory instead of rented across ten tools that never talk. Lobu is where you build it.

For a decade, running a company meant buying software for each job. A tool for sales, a tool for support, a tool for finance, another for the thing the last tool didn't cover. You were not really buying software. You were buying business logic as a product, one vertical at a time. That is starting to come apart, and the reason is how agents get built now. The people who build them have stopped talking about prompts and started talking about loops. They are talking about coding agents, but the idea travels. An agent loop is simple: something happens, the model decides what to do, it does it, and the result feeds the next pass. Once you can build the loop, the loop is the thing you ship. And a loop that watches your data and acts on it is the same business logic a vertical SaaS used to sell you, except you build it once, on one backend, instead of renting ten tools that never share a memory. That is the shift. The workflow layer above your systems of record, the part that used to be a separate tool per function, is turning into agent loops you build. Lobu is the backend you build them on. ## What the loop actually looks like That is one trip around the loop. A payment fails on Acme, the enterprise-churn behavior you defined picks it up, the agent checks the account and drafts a recovery note, and that draft becomes a new event in the log. You define one thing: the behavior. Lobu runs the rest of the circle. Here is each piece. ## Events come in two shapes Push and pull. A webhook posts to Lobu and the payload lands in an append-only events log as a row: Stripe charged a card, a form was submitted, Sentry threw. Or a connector runs on a schedule and goes and gets the data itself, a bank feed, an inbox, a CRM.

<result># Lobu event store — fact sheet (file:line citations against `main`, clean tree)

## 1. The `events` table and append-only discipline

**Schema** — `/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/db/migrations/00000000000000_baseline.sql:847-887`. Key columns (actual names):
- `id bigint` (BIGSERIAL, "exposed to MCP tools" — baseline.sql:899), `organization_id text NOT NULL`
- `entity_ids bigint[]` (:850) — the entity reference is an array, not a single FK
- Provenance: `origin_id`, `origin_parent_id`, `origin_type` ("Source-native item type (post, comment, review, issue, etc.)" — :911), `connector_key`, `connection_id bigint`, `feed_key`, `feed_id`, `run_id`, `client_id`, `created_by`, `source_url`, `author_name`
- Payload: `payload_type` (CHECK: `text|markdown|json_template|media|empty`, :885), `payload_text`, `payload_data jsonb`, `payload_template jsonb`, `attachments jsonb`, `metadata jsonb`
- `semantic_type text DEFAULT 'content' NOT NULL` (:871) — the event-kind column
- Interaction envelope: `interaction_type` (`none|approval`), `interaction_status` (`pending|approved|rejected|completed|failed`), `interaction_input_schema/input/output/error` (:874-879)
- Time: `occurred_at` (when it happened) vs `created_at` (when ingested) (:862-863)
- Supersede: `supersedes_event_id bigint` (:880); generated columns `content_length` and `search_tsv` (weighted tsvector of title+payload_text, :881-882); `score numeric(10,2)` "Normalized 0-100 score for ranking" (:905)
- Embedding lives OFF-table: `event_embeddings (event_id, embedding vector(768), …)` (:940-944), later stamped with `embedding_model` ("Vectors from different stamps are NOT comparable" — `20260526120000_event_embeddings_model_stamp.sql:12`) and re-keyed to `(event, model, chunk)` (`20260618140000_event_embeddings_contract.sql:1-26`).

**Append-only, quoted from the table comment** (baseline.sql:893): *"Append-only event log — the primary data substrate. … Never DELETE; supersede with a tombstone row that points at the original via supersedes_event_id."* Enforced at the DB layer by a BEFORE DELETE trigger `trg_events_append_only` / `events_block_direct_delete()` that raises unless it's an FK cascade or a transaction-scoped `SET LOCAL lobu.allow_event_delete = 'on'` (`20260610040000_events_append_only_guard.sql:28-47`).

**Updates = supersede.** The `current_event_records` view (baseline.sql:950-991) is the live-row read model: events LEFT JOINed to embeddings, filtered by `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM events newer WHERE newer.supersedes_event_id = e.id)`. A partial unique index `idx_events_superseded_by` guarantees at most one superseder per row (concurrent-supersede loser gets a 409 — `save_content.ts:43-56, 433-448`). A denormalized inverse column `superseded_by` was added 2026-07-02 (`20260702200000_events_superseded_by.sql:36-41`): "~75% of rows are superseded" in prod, and the view is planned to flip to `WHERE superseded_by IS NULL` only after an out-of-band backfill — the column is dual-written in the same tx as the superseding INSERT (`insert-event.ts:419-429`), justified as "lineage metadata only, never payload."

## 2. Entities: table + projections, referenced by array + semantic keys

- **Entities are a materialized table, not a pure fold.** `entities` (baseline.sql:1016-1034): per-org rows with `entity_type_id`, jsonb `metadata`, own `content`, `embedding vector(768)`, `content_tsv`, soft-delete. Comment: "Type definition lives in entity_types; the row body is jsonb keyed by the type's columns" (:1040). `entity_types` (:1275-1291) carries `metadata_schema`, **`event_kinds jsonb`** (:1290), `metrics_config`, and `backing_sql`.
- **Derived (view-backed) entity types exist**: "a type is derived iff backing_sql IS NOT NULL … its data comes from running backing_sql via query_sql" (`20260529130000_entity_types_backing.sql:3-14`).
- **An event references entities two ways**: positionally via `events.entity_ids bigint[]`, and semantically via `entity_identities` — normalized `(namespace, identifier)` claims per entity, namespaces like `phone, email, wa_jid, slack_user_id, github_login, auth_user_id` (baseline.sql:1075-1109). `save_content` resolves the caller's `$member` entity through `entity_identities` (auth_user_id, falling back to email then claiming auth_user_id) and appends it to `entity_ids` (`save_content.ts:280-348`); an auto-linker scans content for entity-name mentions post-insert (:451-464).
- **A true event-sourced field fold was tried and deleted**: trigger `project_entity_field` folded `semantic_type='entity_field'` events into `entity_field_state` keep-greater-by-observation_id (`20260623040000_entity_field_grained_projection.sql`), then dropped because "NO read path ever consumed it: entity metadata is still served from the entities.metadata blob"; the already-emitted events stay in the append-only log (`20260623050000_drop_entity_field_projection.sql:3-14`). Don't claim entities are folded from events in the blog — they aren't, currently.
- **`save_content.ts`** (`packages/server/src/tools/save_content.ts`, tool name `save_memory`): `semantic_type` is required and validated against the org's `$member.event_kinds` registry plus entity-type `event_kinds` (:260-274; registry defaults `decision/observation/note/summary/guidance` in `utils/member-entity-type.ts:45-82`; validator in `utils/event-kind-validation.ts:1-10`). The **isOrgGuidance special case** (:207-236): `GUIDANCE_SEMANTIC_TYPE = 'guidance'` (`utils/org-guidance.ts:34`); guidance events are "injected into EVERY agent's system prompt," so authorship is admin/owner-gated as a prompt-injection surface, must be non-empty text/markdown, and superseding a guidance event is gated the same way as deleting it (:369-379).

## 3. Reads: visibility compilation + agent SQL via CTEs

- **`resource-visibility.ts`** (`packages/server/src/authz/resource-visibility.ts:1-113`): "THE generic resource-visibility compiler — gates connector-sourced `events` … by RESOURCE membership … at the `events` read seam." Three-state, composed AND-wise after the per-connection gate: never-graphed connection → passthrough; ACL-enforced connection → event visible only if the requester is `member_of` a `$resource` entity in `events.entity_ids`; graphed-but-stale → **fail closed** ("a stalled sync hides data, it does not leak it", :25).
- **`QUERYABLE_SCHEMA`** (`packages/server/src/utils/table-schema.ts:1-18, 307+): allowlist for `query_sql` — "A column is only safe here if it is EXCLUDED or REDACTED." Embeddings are excluded; `connections.config`/`feeds.config` are redacted in-place by a SQL expression the CTE emits.
- **CTE scoping** (`packages/server/src/utils/execute-data-sources.ts`): `validateAndScopeQuery` (:300-379) parses the SQL, allowlists tables/columns, then `buildScopedQuery` (:391+) wraps **every referenced table in an org-scoped CTE** and prepends one `WITH` block (:724). The `events` CTE reads from `public.current_event_records` (superseded rows already masked) with org scoping matching search (:540-553), then stacks per-user connection visibility + per-resource membership (:576-577). `event_classifications` are gated through their parent event via `current_event_records` "for tombstone parity" (:609-625); `channel_messages` stacks connection visibility + window + per-channel membership (:659-693). **Unknown table names are treated as entity_type slugs** — a CTE over `entities` filtered by `et.slug = $N` (:711-720), which is how derived/custom types are queryable by name.
- Headless/service callers get `principal: null` → "org-visible-only, fail-closed for private data" (:405-416).

## 4. Metric layer

- **Declared, not event-stored**: metric definitions live in `entity_types.metrics_config jsonb` — "eventSets / measures / dimensions / segments … stored verbatim as the author sent it" (`20260615120000_entity_types_metrics_config.sql:3-12`; contract types from `@lobu/connector-sdk` metrics).
- **Compiler** (`packages/server/src/metrics/compiler.ts:1-16`): "lowers a declared metric … into org-scopable SQL over the event stream"; output references `events`/`entities` as plain tables and is passed through `validateAndScopeQuery`, "which rewrites `events` → `current_event_records` (superseded rows masked)" — so metrics automatically read live state. Governing predicates = `segments` (named `where` fragments ANDed in, :81-88); v1 supports `eventSet.by:"alias"` + `reads:"current"` only.
- **Tools**: `list_metrics` is the catalog / "semantic-first discovery step: search here, then query_metric; only fall back to query_sql" (`tools/admin/list_metrics.ts:1-7`); `metric_series` is the "read-only SQL endpoint for dashboard sparklines + stat chips" with the same scoping plus 5s timeout and row cap (`tools/admin/metric_series.ts:1-25`).
- **Dashboard stats are events-sourced**: entity lifecycle changes are recorded as `semantic_type='change'` events — "Used by the metric_series SQL to compute cumulative counts (agents, connections, …) and the dashboard sparklines" (`utils/insert-event.ts:514-586`, esp. the `recordLifecycleEvent` doc at :573-586). Federated warehouse metrics deliberately stay put: "The warehouse stays source of truth; Lobu federates, never re-implements" (`docs/plans/define-metric-design.md:75, 333`).

## 5. Classification / embedding pipeline (one-paragraph version)

A raw event lands via `insertEvent` with a NULL embedding ("Embeddings are left null for background worker backfill" — `save_content.ts:7`); a `*/5` scheduled job creates per-org `embed_backfill` runs that a worker claims to vectorize the recent backlog (`scheduled/trigger-embed-backfill.ts:1-8`, with hard scan bounds after two prod incidents, :28-52). Classifiers (`event_classifiers` + versioned `event_classifier_versions` with `min_similarity`, `preferred_model`, baseline.sql:1369-1426) then label events embedding-first with LLM fallback — `event_classifications.source` CHECK is `embedding|llm|user`, rows carry `values[]`, `confidences`, `met_threshold`, `excerpts` (baseline.sql:1321-1340), with the latest per (event, classifier) exposed via `latest_event_classifications` (:1346, 1535-1548); classification normally runs inline after save, with a scheduled reconciliation as "a FALLBACK mechanism" (`scheduled/classification-reconciliation.ts:1-15`). The result is queryable three ways: FTS (`search_tsv`), vector similarity (`event_embeddings`, model-stamped), and `classification_filters` on retrieval tools (`tools/get_content/handler.ts:242-250`; `utils/content-search/types.ts:55`) — `save_memory` even reports per-row `indexing_status`/`searchable` by probing the same `needsEmbeddingSql` predicate the backfill uses (`save_content.ts:491-513`).

## 6. "Mirror of external systems" framing

There is no single code comment saying "mirror," but the framing is well-supported:
- The events table comment calls each row "a discrete **observation** from a connector or user action" (baseline.sql:893) — observations of external systems, not ownership of them.
- **Sync-in is materialization with supersede semantics**: the connector worker posts item batches; `run-lifecycle.ts:320-348` calls `insertEvent(…, { onConflictUpdate: true })` keyed on `(connection_id, origin_id)` — unchanged item → no-op, changed item → **new row superseding the old** (`insert-event.ts:246, 285-326`), serialized by an advisory lock (:27-47). `feeds` are the sync units: "Per-organization content feeds derived from a connection (e.g., Slack channel → feed, RSS source → feed)" with `checkpoint`, `last_sync_at`, `schedule` (baseline.sql:1449-1483).
- **The strongest "mirror not replace" citation** is the `channel_messages` split (`20260618130000_channel_messages.sql:3-12`): the raw chat transcript is "deliberately NOT the `events` knowledge store … Messages worth remembering are PROMOTED into `events` separately … keeping the knowledge store curated." I.e. events is a curated canonical layer, with the platform remaining the raw archive; the Slack-actions plan states it outright: "Slack is the source of truth; READ-ONLY" (`docs/plans/slack-mcp-agent-actions-and-audience.md:117`).
- For warehouses, external data is **referenced, not materialized**: derived entity types are "`backing`'d by live SQL over the warehouse's OWN semantic view" via connector query pushdown (`docs/plans/define-metric-design.md:72-75, 330-336`).
- Inversely, downstream projections of the event store are explicitly non-canonical: "Postgres/`events` stays canonical; the filesystem (and git) is a projection — a rebuildable read model, never the source of truth" (`docs/plans/knowledge-as-git.md:15`); cold tiering keeps Iceberg as "One source of truth for cold data" (`docs/plans/events-cold-tiering.md:40`).

## Confidence and caveats

**Confidence: high (90)** for sections 1-3 and 5 — every claim is quoted from schema/migration/source read directly this session. **Medium-high (80)** for section 4: I verified declaration storage, compiler, tools, and lifecycle-event sourcing, but did not read the full compiler output SQL or the dashboard frontend that calls `metric_series`. **Medium (70)** for section 6: the "mirror" framing is my synthesis from the cited comments/docs — no literal "mirror" sentence exists in code; the strongest direct quotes are the `channel_messages` migration and the events table comment. Not verified: whether the Stage-2 `superseded_by` view flip has since been applied to prod (the migration says intentionally not committed as a migration file — check `packages/server/src/events/backfill-superseded-by.ts` if it matters); and `docs/plans/*` are design docs, so treat their statements as intent, cross-checked against code where cited.

Suggested next actions: (a) if the blog quotes exact SQL, re-quote from `baseline.sql` at the cited lines rather than my paraphrase; (b) for the classification pipeline, `utils/classification-query.ts` would give the exact embedding-vs-LLM decision logic if you want a deeper paragraph; (c) the `docs/plans/knowledge-as-git.md` "provenance/time-travel as moat" section is strong blog material adjacent to this fact sheet.</result>

The system-type mechanism is a **`$` slug prefix, nothing else**. `/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/core/src/reserved.ts:16-18` — `isSystemEntityType` returns true iff `slug.startsWith("$")`; comment at :13 "platform-owned (hidden from rail, never pruned)". **Only three `$` types exist in code today** (verified by repo-wide sweep of quoted `$`-slugs — only `$member`, `$canvas`, `$resource` appear; `$id` and `$batch_reject` hits are not entity types):

| Slug | Represents | Defined / seeded |

| `$resource` | "ACL-gated access unit (Slack channel, GitHub repository, …). **Important corrections to the prompt's assumed roster:**
- **`$channel` no longer exists.** Migration `/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/db/migrations/20260717120000_system_entity_type_slugs.sql:5-6`: "All ACL access units share ONE entity type: $resource (was channel / repo / $channel / $repo). ## 3. THE invariant: workers never see real credentials

Root statement: `/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/AGENTS.md:15`; refined in `/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/AGENTS.md:28-30`: "Workers never see real credentials. The gateway secret/MCP proxies swap placeholders or inject OAuth/API credentials at egress."

1. **Placeholder mint (gateway-side, at worker spawn)** — `injectSecretPlaceholders` in `/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/orchestration/deployment-manager.ts:1408-1490`: provider credential env vars become `"lobu-proxy"` or a provider-built placeholder (line 1437-1452); any other secret env var is moved into the secret store and replaced by `lobu_secret_<uuid>` via `generatePlaceholder` (line 1454-1476).
2. **The swap seam** — `SecretProxy` in `/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/proxy/secret-proxy.ts:346-355`: "Workers receive random placeholder tokens instead of real secrets. This proxy intercepts requests, swaps placeholders back to real values in auth headers, and forwards to the upstream API." Prefix constant at line 27; the actual swap at `swap()` line 624-661 (fails closed to an empty string so the placeholder never leaks upstream). Placeholders are org-pinned and agent-pinned: `lookupPlaceholderMapping` rejects cross-tenant lookups (line 190-233) and the URL `/a/{agentId}` must match the placeholder's minted agent (line 768-787). Failed resolutions are rate-limited per source (line 54-55).
3. **Forced egress path** — workers can't bypass the proxy: "workers are spawned as child processes of their owner pod and always proxy through `HTTP_PROXY=127.0.0.1:8118`" (secret-proxy.ts:113-117); on Linux the systemd scope's `IPAddressDeny=any` / `IPAddressAllow=127.0.0.1` depends on the proxy binding loopback (`packages/server/AGENTS.md:46`).
4. **App-install tokens** — same invariant, stated in the type contract: "The credential is minted/refreshed gateway-side and never handed to the worker as a raw token — the worker receives a `lobu_secret_<uuid>` placeholder that the secret-proxy swaps at egress" (`connector-types.ts:320-323`); "the private key, the App JWT, and the provider token exchange ALL stay gateway-side" (`/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/installation/installation-token-provider.ts:5-11`).

So the invariant is about **agent workers** (LLM-driven); the first-party **connector-worker fleet** is a trusted platform component that receives resolved connection credentials to run vetted connector code, and **device workers** (user machines) get creds only for connections pinned to that exact device.

---
title: "Event Sourcing for Agents"
description: "The truth stays in Slack, Stripe, and your warehouse. Lobu's memory is an append-only event log that stands in front of them: a governed proxy agents can query, with supersession instead of UPDATE and permissions compiled into every read."
date: 2026-07-28
author: Burak Emre Kabakcı
authorUrl: https://x.com/bu7emba
tags: [architecture, agents, memory, event-sourcing]
draft: false
---

import { TruthProxyDiagram } from "../../components/blog/TruthProxyDiagram";
import { MemberResolutionDiagram } from "../../components/blog/MemberResolutionDiagram";

The industry keeps trying to give agents a single source of truth by building yet another system of record. I think that's backwards. The truth already has homes. Slack owns the conversation, Stripe owns the payment, the warehouse owns revenue. Any product that asks you to move them becomes the thing you migrate away from in two years.

So we built the opposite: a proxy. Lobu's memory is an append-only event log that mirrors the systems you already run. The sources keep the truth. The log keeps the observations, one place every agent reads and writes, with permissions compiled into every query. This is the layer the [landing page](/) calls governed context. Here is how it actually works.

<TruthProxyDiagram />

## Never update, never delete

Every row in the log is an observation: a Slack thread a feed pulled, a payment webhook, a note an agent saved. The comment on the table states the contract: "Never DELETE; supersede with a tombstone row that points at the original." A database trigger blocks deletes outright. Updates don't exist either. Changing a fact means appending a new event that points at the one it replaces, and the read view masks every superseded row. Roughly three quarters of the rows in our production store are superseded. That sounds wasteful right up until you need to know what the agent believed on Tuesday.

Sync follows the same discipline. A feed pulls a thread or a contact. Unchanged items write nothing. Changed items write a new observation that supersedes the old one. And the log is curated, not a data lake: raw chat transcripts deliberately stay out of it, and a message worth remembering gets promoted into an event.

The discipline exists because agents are prolific writers and unreliable editors. Give a fleet of agents UPDATE and you will spend incident reviews reconstructing what got clobbered. Give them supersession and every mistake is one pointer away from undone. Provenance stops being a feature. It is the storage format, and every action an agent takes lands back in the log as one more event.

## The entities we ship

Entities live next to the log: companies, deals, goals, whatever your config declares. Agents query them by name. An unknown table in an agent's SQL resolves as an entity type, so `SELECT name FROM company` just works, scoped to your org and your permissions. A few types ship with the platform, prefixed with `$`, and they do the governance work.

`$member` is a person. The same human shows up as a Slack user id, an email address, a web login. Each one is an identity claim in a single table, and the claims resolve onto one member entity. Sign in with an identity a sync already saw and the claim moves onto your member. Two members claiming the same identity is a conflict we refuse to guess about: that's two humans and one Slack id, and nothing merges. Merging is an explicit operation, logged and reversible, and the log itself is never rewritten.

<MemberResolutionDiagram />

`$resource` is the access-control anchor. A Slack channel and a GitHub repo are the same kind of thing: a unit of access, with membership edges synced from the source. An agent recalls a channel's history only for someone whose member entity is a member of that channel. When the membership sync goes stale, the gate fails closed. A stalled sync hides data. It does not leak it.

Metrics are the deliberate exception, because a metric should not be a row anyone edits. A metric is a declared definition on an entity type: measures over event sets, with named segments, compiled into the same org-scoped SQL every other read uses. Declare `asset.spend` once and the dashboard sparkline, the agent's answer, and your goal tracking compute the same number from the same events. Even the dashboard is event-sourced: lifecycle changes are themselves events, and the stats fold over them.

## Who holds the keys

Everything enters and leaves through connectors. Feeds pull data in on a schedule or receive webhooks, actions push changes out. Auth is whatever the source demands: managed OAuth, your own OAuth app, API keys, org-level app installs, a paired browser extension riding a session you're already signed into, or a connector pinned to a specific device. With managed OAuth the client secret and refresh token never leave our cloud; your instance receives an access token and its expiry, nothing more. At rest, credentials are AES-256-GCM encrypted and scoped per organization.

The invariant we hold hardest: an agent worker never sees a real credential. Workers get placeholder tokens. A proxy at the network edge swaps the placeholder for the real value as the request leaves the box, and the worker's egress is forced through that proxy, so the secret only ever exists outside the sandbox. App-install private keys and token exchanges never leave the gateway at all. The one exception is deliberate: a connection pinned to your own device runs with that device's credentials, because that is exactly what you authorized when you bound it.

Privacy rides the same read path as everything else. A connection backed by a personal OAuth login is forced private, enforced by a database trigger, so your Gmail cannot surface in a coworker's recall no matter what an agent asks. Writes are gated too. Actions declare whether they read or write, a write can require human approval, org policy can force approval or deny outright, and an unapproved run is structurally unclaimable: there is no code path by which a worker picks it up.

## A proxy is the honest name

We could market this as the single source of truth for agents. It isn't, and it shouldn't be. The truth stays in the systems that own it. The log keeps what was observed, who may see it, and what the agent did about it, and that compounds into the one thing the sources can't give you: a governed memory every agent shares.

Start with the [docs](/getting-started/), or read how the [memory layer](/getting-started/memory/) works.

title: "Self-Improving Agents Are Event-Sourced"
description: "An agent improves when its next run can see what the last run did and what happened after. That is a storage problem before it is a model problem, and the storage is an append-only event log that proxies your systems of record."
date: 2026-07-28

import { TruthProxyDiagram } from "../../components/blog/TruthProxyDiagram";
import { MemberResolutionDiagram } from "../../components/blog/MemberResolutionDiagram";

Everyone wants self-improving agents, and the fashionable answers are model-side: reflection loops, fine-tuning, memory frameworks with philosophical names. I think the answer is boring. It is event sourcing. An agent improves when its next run can see what the last run did, what a human said about it, and what happened after. That is a storage problem before it is a model problem.

The storage cannot be another system of record, though. The truth already has homes. Slack owns the conversation, Stripe owns the payment, the warehouse owns revenue, and any product that asks you to move them becomes the thing you migrate away from in two years. So we built a proxy instead. Lobu's memory is an append-only event log that mirrors the systems you already run. The sources keep the truth. The log keeps the observations, one place every agent reads and writes, with permissions compiled into every query.

## Never update, never delete

Every row in the log is an observation: a Slack thread a feed pulled, a payment webhook, a note an agent saved. Changing a fact means appending a new event that points at the one it replaces, and the read view masks every superseded row. Roughly three quarters of the rows in our production store are superseded. That sounds wasteful right up until you need to know what the agent believed on Tuesday.

And the log is curated, not a data lake: raw chat transcripts deliberately stay out of it, and a message worth remembering gets promoted into an event.

The discipline exists because agents are prolific writers and unreliable editors. Give a fleet of agents UPDATE and you will spend incident reviews reconstructing what got clobbered. Give them supersession and every mistake is one pointer away from undone. Provenance stops being a feature. It is the storage format.

Everything enters and leaves through connectors. Feeds pull data in on a schedule or receive webhooks, actions push changes out. Privacy rides the same read path as everything else. A connection backed by a personal OAuth login is forced private, enforced by a database trigger, so your Gmail cannot surface in a coworker's recall no matter what an agent asks.

Consequential writes are where most agent platforms bolt on an approval queue. Ours is the log again. When an agent wants to do something gated, one transaction writes a pending run and a pending approval event.
